gloss_terse: To penetrate, pierce through, pass completely through something, especially in a physical or metaphorical sense
gloss_readable: This verb describes the action of penetrating or passing through something completely. In Hebrews 4:12, it vividly portrays God's word as sharper than any double-edged sword, piercing so deeply it divides soul from spirit. The Greek carries a sense of thorough, complete penetration—not merely touching the surface but reaching the innermost parts. Classical uses include missiles reaching their target or time intervals passing through.

senses.1: The single New Testament occurrence (Heb 4:12) uses this term metaphorically for the word of God 'piercing' to the division of soul and spirit. The multilingual glosses emphasize penetration and piercing, reflecting the word's fundamental sense of going completely through something. Classical Greek uses it for physical piercing with missiles or reaching a destination through obstacles.

gloss_terse: Righteous judgment, just verdict, fair and equitable decision rendered according to divine or moral standards
gloss_readable: A compound noun combining 'righteous' (δίκαιος) and 'judgment' (κρίσις), this term refers to judgment that is inherently fair and morally upright. Paul uses it in Romans 2:5 to describe the day of God's righteous judgment when His just verdicts will be revealed. The word emphasizes not merely any judgment, but specifically one that is ethically sound and divinely authorized. It appears in contexts where the justice of God's decisions is being emphasized.

senses.1: Romans 2:5 speaks of the revelation of God's righteous judgment on the day of wrath. The term combines the concepts of justice and judgment, stressing the moral uprightness of God's verdicts. Spanish 'justo juicio,' French 'juste jugement,' and German 'gerechtes Gericht' all preserve this dual emphasis on both the judicial act and its righteous character.

gloss_terse: Double-tongued, saying one thing to one person and another to someone else; deceitful in speech
gloss_readable: This adjective literally means 'of double word' and describes someone who speaks duplicitously, telling different stories to different people. In 1 Timothy 3:8, Paul lists this among disqualifying traits for deacons—church servants must not be two-faced in their communication. The image is of a forked tongue, speaking contradictory things. It's not merely changing one's mind, but deliberately deceiving through inconsistent speech designed to manipulate different audiences.

senses.1: Paul's instruction to Timothy (1 Tim 3:8) requires deacons not to be double-tongued—speaking one way to one group and differently to another for manipulative purposes. The English and Spanish glosses capture the 'double word/speech' imagery, while the French preserves the Greek transliteration. This describes deliberate duplicity in communication, a fundamental breach of trustworthiness required for church leadership.

gloss_terse: Dionysius, personal name meaning 'of Dionysus' or 'follower of Dionysus,' an Athenian convert
gloss_readable: Dionysius was an Athenian who became a believer through Paul's ministry on the Areopagus (Acts 17:34). His name derives from Dionysus, the Greek god of wine, reflecting the pagan naming conventions of ancient Athens. Early Christian tradition identifies him as the first bishop of Athens, though this cannot be verified from Scripture alone. The brief mention in Acts suggests he was a person of some standing, converted alongside Damaris and others.

senses.1: Acts 17:34 mentions Dionysius as one of the Athenian converts from Paul's Areopagus speech. His theophoric name (derived from the god Dionysus) was common in Greek culture. The multilingual glosses largely preserve the Greek form, with French rendering it as 'Denys.' Luke's inclusion of his name suggests he became a notable member of the Athenian Christian community.

gloss_terse: Fallen from Zeus, fallen from the sky; said of sacred objects believed to have divine heavenly origin
gloss_readable: This rare adjective literally means 'fallen from Zeus' and was used in the ancient world to describe objects—especially cult images—believed to have fallen from heaven as gifts from the gods. In Acts 19:35, the Ephesian town clerk uses it to describe the image of Artemis housed in her famous temple. The claim that the idol 'fell from heaven' authenticated its divine origin in pagan thinking. The term reflects ancient religious belief that certain sacred objects had supernatural, celestial origins.

senses.1: The Ephesian town clerk (Acts 19:35) calms the riot by affirming that all know Ephesus guards the temple of Artemis and the image 'fallen from Zeus' (i.e., from heaven). This reflects ancient pagan belief in meteorite-origin cult images or divinely sent idols. Spanish 'caída del cielo' (fallen from heaven) and French 'tombé du ciel' capture the sense better than literal 'Zeus' reference, as the phrase functioned as a claim of heavenly divine origin.

gloss_terse: The Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux), twin sons of Zeus, patron deities of sailors, constellation Gemini
gloss_readable: The Dioscuri—literally 'sons of Zeus'—were the divine twins Castor and Pollux (Greek Polydeuces), born to Leda. In Greco-Roman religion, they were patron gods of sailors, believed to protect ships and appear as the electrical phenomenon St. Elmo's fire during storms. Acts 28:11 mentions them as the figurehead of the Alexandrian ship that carried Paul from Malta to Italy. Ships often bore images of patron deities on their prows, and the Dioscuri were especially popular for Mediterranean vessels.

senses.1: Acts 28:11 identifies Paul's ship by its figurehead: the Dioscuri, the twin gods Castor and Pollux who protected sailors in Greek and Roman belief. Ship figureheads invoked divine protection for voyages. French 'Dioscures' and English transliterations preserve the Greek, while Spanish maintains the Greek form. The reference shows how pagan religious symbols pervaded ancient maritime culture.

gloss_terse: Diotrephes, personal name meaning 'nourished by Zeus,' an early church leader who loved preeminence
gloss_readable: Diotrephes appears only in 3 John 9 as a church leader who opposed the apostle John's authority and refused to welcome traveling missionaries. His name means 'nourished/cherished by Zeus,' a common Greek theophoric name. John criticizes him for loving to have the preeminence, spreading malicious gossip about the apostles, and excommunicating those who showed hospitality to John's messengers. He represents early church power struggles and the danger of authoritarianism divorced from apostolic teaching.

senses.1: 3 John 9 mentions Diotrephes as someone who 'loves to be first' and rejects apostolic authority. His Zeus-derived name was typical in Greek culture. John's critique reveals early church conflict between local leaders and apostolic oversight. The multilingual glosses preserve the Greek name with various transliterations, as it's a proper noun referring to a specific individual who embodied self-promotion over submission to apostolic teaching.

gloss_terse: To double, multiply by two, repeat twofold; to repay double the amount
gloss_readable: This verb means to make double or to multiply by two. In Revelation 18:6, it appears in the command concerning Babylon: 'Repay her double according to her works.' The doubling represents proportional justice—she receives back twice what she dealt out, emphasizing the completeness of divine retribution. Classical Greek used it for doubling quantities, folding garments in half, or repaying debts with interest. The New Testament usage carries the sense of comprehensive, multiplied judgment matching the scale of transgression.

senses.1: Revelation 18:6 commands that Babylon be repaid 'double' (doubled) for her deeds, a vivid image of comprehensive divine justice. The Greek concept involves multiplying by two or repeating something twofold. English 'double,' Spanish 'doblad,' French and German 'verdoppeln' all capture the mathematical and retributive sense: complete payback multiplied, leaving nothing unaccounted for in God's judgment against the symbolic evil city.

gloss_terse: Two thousand, the number 2,000; a specific quantity in the thousands range
gloss_readable: A straightforward numerical term meaning two thousand. Mark 5:13 uses it to describe the size of the herd of pigs into which Jesus permitted the demons to enter—about two thousand swine rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned. The specific number emphasizes the magnitude of both the demonic possession (the demons were called 'Legion') and the economic loss to the swineherds. Greek numerical adjectives like this one were standard vocabulary for counting and measurement.

senses.1: Mark 5:13 specifies that about two thousand pigs drowned after Jesus cast the demons into them. The precise number underscores the enormous scale of the miracle and the economic impact on the region. All language traditions render this straightforwardly as 'two thousand'—English, Spanish 'dos mil,' French 'deux mille,' German 'zweitausend'—as it's a simple numerical designation requiring no cultural translation beyond the number system itself.

gloss_terse: To strain out, filter carefully, remove small particles by passing through a filter; metaphor for scrupulosity
gloss_readable: This verb means to strain or filter thoroughly, removing tiny particles from liquid. Jesus uses it memorably in Matthew 23:24 when He accuses the scribes and Pharisees of 'straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel'—being meticulously careful about minor ritual matters while ignoring massive moral failures. The image comes from wine-making and water purification practices where gnats or other small impurities were filtered out. Classical Greek used it for careful filtering of wine or other liquids.

senses.1: Matthew 23:24 presents Jesus' biting critique: the religious leaders strain out gnats (tiny ritually unclean insects) while swallowing camels (massive unclean animals). The verb describes careful filtering to remove minute particles, used metaphorically for obsessive attention to minor legal details. Spanish 'coláis,' French 'filtrer,' and English 'straining out' all capture the filtering imagery—meticulous removal of the tiniest impurities while missing catastrophic contamination.

gloss_terse: To divide in two, separate, set at variance; to cause division or discord between people
gloss_readable: This verb fundamentally means to divide something into two parts or to split in half. Matthew 10:35 uses it in Jesus' sobering prophecy that He came 'to set a man against his father'—His message would create division even within families. The term can describe physical division or, metaphorically, relational separation and conflict. Classical Greek used it for literally cutting things in two or for creating divisions at midday (the day being 'split'). The New Testament usage emphasizes the divisive social impact of allegiance to Christ.

senses.1: Matthew 10:35 uses this verb for Jesus' purpose 'to divide'—to set family members against each other through the radical claims of discipleship. The term conveys separation into two opposing parts. English 'to divide,' Spanish 'dividir,' French 'diviser' all express this fundamental splitting. Jesus' statement acknowledges that following Him creates unavoidable divisions when some accept and others reject His call, even breaking family unity.

gloss_terse: Thirst, the physical condition of needing water; craving for drink, dehydration
gloss_readable: A straightforward noun for the physical experience of thirst—the body's need for water. Paul lists it in 2 Corinthians 11:27 among his apostolic sufferings: hunger and thirst were part of the hardships he endured for the gospel. While Scripture also uses thirst metaphorically for spiritual longing (as Jesus does in John 4), this particular occurrence refers to literal physical deprivation. The term appears in both classical Greek and the Septuagint for the common human experience of needing to drink.

senses.1: 2 Corinthians 11:27 includes thirst in Paul's catalog of hardships—alongside hunger, cold, and nakedness. This is literal physical thirst, the body's craving for water during difficult missionary journeys. All language traditions use their standard word for this universal human experience: English 'thirst,' Spanish 'sed,' French 'soif,' German 'Durst.' Paul's willingness to endure such basic physical deprivation demonstrates his commitment to gospel ministry above personal comfort.

gloss_terse: Persecutor, one who pursues others with intent to harm, harasser of the faithful
gloss_readable: This noun designates someone who pursues others to harm them—a persecutor or hunter of people. Paul uses it of himself in 1 Timothy 1:13, confessing that before his conversion he was 'a blasphemer, persecutor, and violent aggressor' against the church. The term derives from the verb 'to pursue' or 'chase,' carrying connotations of hunting down prey. Paul's self-description emphasizes the magnitude of God's mercy—even a violent persecutor of Christians could be transformed into Christ's apostle.

senses.1: 1 Timothy 1:13 records Paul's confession that he was formerly a persecutor of the church, someone who actively hunted down believers. The Greek emphasizes aggressive pursuit with hostile intent. English 'persecutor' and Spanish 'perseguidor' capture this sense of one who chases down victims. Paul's candid acknowledgment of his pre-conversion violence against Christians magnifies the grace that transformed him from Christianity's chief enemy to its greatest missionary.

gloss_terse: To submit to rules or regulations, be subject to ordinances, accept imposed decrees
gloss_readable: This verb in the passive voice means to submit oneself to decrees, ordinances, or regulations. Paul uses it in Colossians 2:20 to challenge the Colossians: if you died with Christ to the elemental principles of the world, why do you submit to regulations as if still living in the world? The term emphasizes voluntary submission to imposed rules or decrees. Classical Greek used it for establishing decrees or, in the passive, being governed by them. Paul questions why believers would return to rule-based religion after experiencing freedom in Christ.

senses.1: Colossians 2:20 questions why believers submit to regulations ('Do not handle, Do not taste') when they've died with Christ to worldly principles. The verb emphasizes accepting or subjecting oneself to imposed rules. Spanish 'sometéis a decretos' and English 'submit to rules' capture this sense of voluntary compliance with external ordinances. Paul challenges the Colossians' return to legalistic religion that contradicts their freedom and completeness in Christ.

gloss_terse: Deceitful, crafty, treacherous; characterized by cunning and deceptive intent
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning crafty, deceitful, or treacherous—describing someone who operates through cunning and deception rather than honesty. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 11:13 to describe false apostles as 'deceitful workers' who disguise themselves as apostles of Christ. Classical Greek applied it to treacherous persons, cunning schemes, or even deities like Hermes and Aphrodite known for trickery. The term emphasizes deliberate, calculated deception designed to mislead others for selfish gain.

senses.1: 2 Corinthians 11:13 identifies Paul's opponents as 'deceitful workers' masquerading as genuine apostles. The adjective describes those who work through cunning manipulation and deception. English 'deceitful,' Spanish 'engañosos,' French 'trompeur,' and German 'betrügerisch' all emphasize the fraudulent, treacherous character of these false teachers. Their craftiness involves deliberate misrepresentation—appearing righteous while serving selfish or demonic purposes rather than Christ.

gloss_terse: To deal treacherously, deceive, act with guile; to behave deceitfully toward others
gloss_readable: This verb means to act treacherously or deal deceitfully with someone. Romans 3:13 quotes Psalm 5:9 in Paul's catalog of universal human sinfulness: 'they kept deceiving with their tongues.' The term emphasizes ongoing deceptive behavior and treacherous dealing. The Septuagint uses it for acting with guile or betraying trust. Classical Greek similarly employed it for treacherous conduct. Paul's use highlights the moral corruption of humanity—speech itself becomes an instrument of deception and betrayal.

senses.1: Romans 3:13 cites the Septuagint: 'they were deceiving with their tongues'—the imperfect tense suggesting continuous treacherous action. The verb describes dealing deceitfully or acting with guile toward others. Spanish 'engañaban,' French 'user de ruse,' and German 'betrügen' all emphasize the fraudulent, faithless character of fallen human speech. Paul employs this Old Testament quotation to demonstrate that universal sinfulness includes habitual deception in communication.

gloss_terse: To adulterate, falsify, corrupt by mixing; to handle deceitfully or manipulate dishonestly
gloss_readable: This verb means to adulterate, corrupt, or handle something deceitfully—like a merchant mixing inferior materials into a product to defraud customers. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 4:2, renouncing 'adulterating the word of God'—he refuses to corrupt or manipulate God's message for personal gain. Classical Greek used it for adulterating wine, alloying metals with cheaper substances, or disguising things deceptively. Paul contrasts such corruption with proclaiming truth openly and honestly.

senses.1: 2 Corinthians 4:2 has Paul renouncing the practice of 'adulterating the word of God'—corrupting or manipulating Scripture for selfish purposes. The verb describes mixing in foreign elements to defraud, like diluting wine or alloying gold. Spanish 'adulterando,' French 'falsifier,' and English 'adulterating' capture this sense of corrupt handling that compromises purity. Paul insists on transparent, honest proclamation rather than crafty manipulation of God's truth.

gloss_terse: Giver, one who gives, donor; a person characterized by generosity and giving
gloss_readable: A straightforward noun meaning 'giver'—one who gives or donates. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 9:7 in his famous statement: 'God loves a cheerful giver.' The term emphasizes not merely the act of giving but the person characterized by generosity. It's a later Greek form related to the verb 'to give.' Paul's point is that God values not the amount given but the heart attitude—cheerful willingness rather than grudging obligation. The giver's disposition matters more than the gift's size.

senses.1: 2 Corinthians 9:7 declares God's love for a 'cheerful giver'—one whose giving flows from joy rather than compulsion. The noun emphasizes the person's character as one who gives. All languages render this transparently: English 'giver,' Spanish 'dador,' French 'donateur,' German 'Geber.' Paul's teaching elevates generous disposition over mechanical obligation—God delights in those whose giving reflects inner joy and love rather than external pressure or duty.

gloss_terse: To treat as a slave, bring into subjection, discipline severely; to exercise strict control over
gloss_readable: This verb means to enslave, subjugate, or bring under strict discipline—literally to treat something as a slave. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 9:27 describing his self-discipline: 'I discipline my body and bring it into subjection.' The image is of an athlete or fighter exercising rigorous control over physical impulses to achieve a goal. Classical Greek used it for reducing someone to slavery or exercising harsh control. Paul applies it to voluntary self-mastery—treating his body as a slave to ensure his ministry's effectiveness.

senses.1: 1 Corinthians 9:27 has Paul declaring he disciplines his body and 'brings it into subjection'—exercising strict mastery over physical desires like an athlete in training. The verb carries the force of enslaving or subjugating. Spanish 'esclavizo,' French 'réduire en esclavage,' and English 'bring into subjection' all capture this harsh control imagery. Paul's voluntary self-discipline prevents his body's appetites from disqualifying him from the very gospel he preaches to others.

gloss_terse: To grasp, seize with the hand, catch hold of; to take firmly in one's grip
gloss_readable: This middle voice verb means to grasp or seize something with the hand—to take firm hold. In 1 Corinthians 3:19, Paul quotes Job 5:13: God 'catches the wise in their craftiness.' The image is of God grasping cunning schemers as one might grab an opponent. Classical Greek used it for clutching handfuls of something or seizing someone by the throat. The New Testament usage emphasizes God's power to capture and thwart those who rely on their own cleverness rather than His wisdom.

senses.1: 1 Corinthians 3:19 quotes Job's declaration that God 'catches the wise in their craftiness'—seizing them in the very schemes they devise. The verb describes grasping firmly with the hand, like catching prey. English 'catching,' Spanish 'atrapando,' French 'saisir,' and German 'fangen' all express this sense of firm seizure. God turns human cunning back on itself, grasping schemers in their own traps—divine wisdom defeats worldly cleverness at its own game.

gloss_terse: Drusilla, Roman personal name; wife of Felix the governor, daughter of Herod Agrippa I
gloss_readable: Drusilla was the wife of the Roman procurator Felix, present when Paul reasoned about faith in Christ (Acts 24:24). She was the daughter of Herod Agrippa I and great-granddaughter of Herod the Great. Her name is Latin, from the Drusus family. Historically, she left her first husband to marry Felix, a scandal noted by Josephus. Luke's mention of her suggests both she and Felix heard Paul's gospel presentation, though their response was to postpone further discussion out of fear.

senses.1: Acts 24:24 identifies Drusilla as Felix's wife (herself Jewish, daughter of Herod Agrippa I) who was present for Paul's testimony. Her Latin name reflects Roman cultural dominance. French 'Drusille' naturalizes it slightly, while other languages preserve the Greek transliteration. Her presence during Paul's discussion of 'righteousness, self-control, and judgment' may have been particularly uncomfortable given her questionable marriage to Felix, possibly contributing to their fearful response.

gloss_terse: Dysentery, severe intestinal inflammation causing diarrhea and bleeding; a specific medical condition
gloss_readable: A medical term for dysentery—severe inflammation of the intestines causing bloody diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain. Acts 28:8 describes Publius's father suffering from fever and dysentery when Paul healed him on Malta. The term was used in classical medical writings by Hippocrates and others for this specific disease. Luke, the physician-evangelist, employs the precise medical vocabulary of his day. The healing demonstrates Christ's power over disease and opened doors for ministry on the island.

senses.1: Acts 28:8 records that Publius's father lay sick with fever and dysentery, a serious intestinal disease causing severe diarrhea and dehydration. Luke uses the technical medical term familiar from Hippocratic writings. All modern languages preserve medical terminology: English 'dysentery,' Spanish 'disentería,' French 'dysenterie.' Paul's healing of this dangerous condition through prayer demonstrated divine power and led to widespread healing ministry on Malta, opening the community to the gospel.

gloss_terse: Hard to interpret, difficult to explain, not easily understood or communicated
gloss_readable: This adjective means difficult to interpret, explain, or express—something challenging to make clear to others. Hebrews 5:11 uses it when the author says certain teachings about Melchizedek are 'hard to explain' because the readers have become dull of hearing. Classical Greek also used it for things hard to describe or interpret. The difficulty isn't in the subject itself but in communicating it to an unprepared or inattentive audience. The author's frustration points to the readers' spiritual immaturity, not the doctrine's inherent obscurity.

senses.1: Hebrews 5:11 acknowledges that teaching about Melchizedek's priesthood is 'hard to explain'—not because it's impossibly complex, but because the audience has become 'dull of hearing.' The adjective describes something difficult to interpret or express clearly. Spanish 'difícil de explicar,' French 'difficile à expliquer,' and English 'hard to explain' all capture this communication challenge. The author's concern is pedagogical—spiritual dullness makes even important truths hard to convey effectively.

gloss_terse: Difficult, hard to accomplish, troublesome; presenting challenges or obstacles
gloss_readable: This adjective means difficult, hard, or troublesome—describing something that presents challenges. Mark 10:24 uses it when Jesus says 'how difficult it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God.' Classical Greek used it for people hard to please, situations that are troublesome, or tasks difficult to accomplish. The term emphasizes objective difficulty, not impossibility. Jesus' teaching addresses the genuine challenge wealth poses to discipleship—riches tempt self-reliance, making dependence on God psychologically difficult.

senses.1: Mark 10:24 records Jesus' observation that it's 'difficult' for the wealthy to enter God's kingdom. The adjective describes something genuinely hard or troublesome, though not impossible. English 'difficult,' Spanish 'difícil,' French and German 'difficile/schwer' all express this challenge. The disciples' astonishment at Jesus' statement shows they assumed wealth indicated God's blessing—Jesus corrects this, showing that riches create spiritual obstacles by fostering self-sufficiency that resists childlike dependence on God.

gloss_terse: Hard to understand, difficult to grasp intellectually; not easily comprehended
gloss_readable: This adjective describes something intellectually difficult to grasp or understand. In 2 Peter 3:16, Peter acknowledges that some things in Paul's letters are 'hard to understand,' which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction. Classical Greek used it for things difficult to comprehend. Peter's candid admission validates the intellectual challenge of some biblical teaching while warning against using difficulty as license for distortion. Difficulty requires diligent study, not revision to match our preferences.

senses.1: 2 Peter 3:16 admits that some of Paul's writings contain things 'hard to understand,' which unstable people distort. The adjective emphasizes intellectual difficulty in grasping meaning. Spanish 'difíciles de entender,' French preserves the Greek form, and English 'hard to understand' all acknowledge genuine comprehension challenges. Peter doesn't excuse confusion but warns that difficulty makes Scripture vulnerable to misinterpretation by those unwilling to do careful study—twisted teaching often exploits genuinely complex passages.

gloss_terse: Twelfth, the ordinal number for position twelve in a sequence
gloss_readable: The ordinal number 'twelfth'—indicating the twelfth position in a sequence. Revelation 21:20 uses it to describe the twelfth foundation of the New Jerusalem, which is adorned with amethyst. This is straightforward numerical vocabulary with no special theological significance beyond the symbolic completeness of twelve (tribes, apostles) in biblical numerology. Greek ordinal numbers function like their English equivalents for indicating position or order.

senses.1: Revelation 21:20 identifies the twelfth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem as amethyst. This is simple ordinal numbering—the final in the sequence of twelve foundations representing the twelve apostles. All languages render it straightforwardly: English 'twelfth,' Spanish 'duodécimo,' French 'douzième,' German 'zwölfte.' The number twelve throughout Revelation symbolizes completeness and the people of God—twelve tribes, twelve gates, twelve foundations, twelve apostles of the Lamb.

gloss_terse: The twelve tribes, collective designation for the tribes of Israel as a unified whole
gloss_readable: A compound adjective meaning 'of twelve tribes,' used as a noun for the collective people of Israel. Acts 26:7 has Paul speak of 'our twelve tribes' earnestly serving God day and night, hoping to attain the promise. Though ten tribes had been scattered centuries earlier, Judaism maintained the concept of the unified twelve-tribe nation. The term emphasizes Israel's corporate identity as God's covenant people. Paul's usage shows the resurrection hope was fundamentally Jewish, not a new religion.

senses.1: Acts 26:7 has Paul referencing 'our twelve tribes' serving God in hope of the resurrection promise. The term designates Israel collectively as the complete nation of twelve tribes, despite historical dispersion. English 'twelve tribes,' Spanish 'doce tribus,' and French 'douze tribus' all maintain this numerical-ethnic designation. Paul's reference affirms continuity between Israel's ancient hope and Christian resurrection faith—Jesus fulfills Jewish promises, not replacing but completing Israel's story.

gloss_terse: Ha! An exclamation expressing surprise, recognition, fear, or protest; an interjection
gloss_readable: An exclamation or interjection expressing sudden emotion—surprise, recognition, fear, or protest. In Luke 4:34, the demon-possessed man cries out 'Ha! What have we to do with You, Jesus of Nazareth?' The particle often introduces a challenge or expresses alarm. It's the verbal equivalent of a startled reaction. Demonic spirits frequently use it in the Gospels when confronted by Jesus—recognizing His identity and authority while protesting His interference. It's an involuntary outburst revealing inner disturbance.

senses.1: Luke 4:34 records the demoniac's outburst: 'Ha! What do we have to do with You, Jesus?'—the demon recognizing Jesus and protesting His intervention. The interjection expresses alarm, surprise, or recognition. Spanish '¡Ah!,' French 'Ah!,' and English 'Ha!' all convey this sudden exclamation. The demon's involuntary outcry reveals both supernatural recognition of Jesus' identity and fear of His authority—spiritual beings cannot remain neutral when confronted by the Son of God.

gloss_terse: Seventy times, an adverbial number indicating repetition seventy times over
gloss_readable: An adverb meaning 'seventy times'—indicating frequency or repetition. Matthew 18:22 uses it in Jesus' response to Peter's question about forgiveness: not just seven times, but 'seventy times seven' (or 'seventy-seven times' depending on interpretation). Either reading means unlimited forgiveness. The number echoes Genesis 4:24, where Lamech boasts of vengeance seventy-sevenfold—Jesus transforms vengeance into forgiveness. The hyperbolic number isn't meant for literal counting but expresses boundless, inexhaustible grace.

senses.1: Matthew 18:22 has Jesus telling Peter to forgive 'seventy times seven'—a number so large it means unlimited forgiveness, not literal tallying. The adverb emphasizes repeated action. Most translations preserve the numerical form: English 'seventy times,' Spanish 'setenta veces,' French 'soixante-dix fois.' Jesus deliberately reverses Lamech's boast of multiplied vengeance (Gen 4:24), transforming the mathematics of revenge into the mathematics of grace—forgiveness without limit or calculation.

gloss_terse: Eber, Hebrew ancestor of Abraham, from whom 'Hebrew' may derive; patriarch in Genesis genealogy
gloss_readable: Eber (Hebrew עֵבֶר) was a descendant of Shem and ancestor of Abraham, appearing in the genealogies of Genesis 10-11 and Luke 3:35. His name may be the origin of the term 'Hebrew' (Ibri), designating Abraham's people as 'descendants of Eber.' He lived during the time of the Tower of Babel and the division of languages. Luke includes him in Jesus' genealogy, tracing Christ's lineage back through Israel's patriarchal line to Adam. The name signifies 'the one from beyond' (the Euphrates).

senses.1: Luke 3:35 includes Eber in Jesus' genealogy, linking Christ to the Hebrew patriarchs descended from Shem. His name may etymologically connect to 'Hebrew' as an ethnic designation. All languages largely preserve the Hebrew name: English 'Eber,' Spanish 'Éber,' French 'Éber.' Luke's genealogical precision demonstrates Jesus' authentic placement within Israel's historical lineage, tracing His human descent through Abraham's ancestors back to Noah and ultimately Adam, showing Him as both Israel's King and humanity's Savior.

gloss_terse: Hebrew, pertaining to the Hebrew language or the Jewish people and their culture
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning 'Hebrew'—pertaining to the Hebrew language or Jewish culture. Luke 23:38 (in some manuscripts) describes Pilate's inscription on the cross being written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—the three major languages of first-century Judea. Hebrew (or Aramaic, its related dialect) was the ethnic language of the Jewish people, Greek the international trade language, and Latin the imperial Roman tongue. The trilingual inscription proclaimed Jesus' kingship to all cultural groups present in Jerusalem.

senses.1: Luke 23:38 (in certain manuscripts) notes the cross inscription was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. The adjective designates the language/script of the Jewish people. Spanish 'Hebreas,' French 'en hébreu,' and English 'Hebrew' all refer to the Semitic language. The trilingual proclamation ensured maximum readership—Jewish pilgrims, Greek-speaking gentiles, and Roman officials could all read that Jesus was crucified as 'King of the Jews,' ironically proclaiming truth in the act of mockery.

gloss_terse: Guarantee, surety, one who pledges security for another; bondsman ensuring fulfillment
gloss_readable: This noun means a guarantee, surety, or bondsman—one who pledges to ensure another's obligation is fulfilled. Hebrews 7:22 declares Jesus the 'guarantee of a better covenant,' meaning He personally ensures all covenant promises will be kept. Classical Greek used it for someone providing financial security or bail. Unlike the old covenant depending on human faithfulness (which failed), the new covenant rests on Jesus' perfect guarantee—His own person and work secure what He promises. He is both promise-maker and promise-keeper.

senses.1: Hebrews 7:22 calls Jesus the 'guarantee' of a better covenant—He Himself secures all its promises through His priestly work. The noun describes a bondsman or surety who pledges to ensure obligations are met. English 'guarantee,' Spanish 'garante,' French 'garant,' and German 'Bürge' all convey this security function. Unlike the Levitical priests who died and failed, Jesus lives forever and perfectly guarantees the new covenant—His resurrection life ensures every promise finds fulfillment.

gloss_terse: Nearer, closer in space or time; comparative form indicating reduced distance
gloss_readable: The comparative adverb 'nearer' or 'closer'—indicating proximity in space or time. Romans 13:11 uses it temporally: 'salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed.' Paul emphasizes the forward progress of redemptive history—each day brings believers closer to Christ's return and the consummation of salvation. The comparative form stresses movement toward a goal. Time isn't cyclical but linear, advancing toward the day when faith becomes sight and hope becomes reality.

senses.1: Romans 13:11 declares that salvation is 'nearer' now than when believers first trusted Christ—the return of the Lord draws progressively closer. The comparative adverb indicates reduced distance or time. Spanish 'más cerca,' French 'plus près,' German 'näher,' and English 'nearer' all express this approach toward a goal. Paul's point motivates urgent holiness—the eschatological clock is ticking, Christ's return approaches, making moral vigilance increasingly critical as the end draws near.

gloss_terse: Raising, resurrection; the act of waking or raising from sleep or death
gloss_readable: This noun means raising, awakening, or resurrection—the act of bringing someone up from sleep or death. Matthew 27:53 uses it for the resurrection of saints who came out of tombs 'after His resurrection' and appeared to many. The term can mean simple awakening from sleep or, more significantly, resurrection from death. It derives from the verb 'to raise' or 'awaken.' Matthew's reference connects Jesus' resurrection to the resurrection of Old Testament believers, showing His death and rising as the pivot point for all resurrection hope.

senses.1: Matthew 27:53 describes saints rising from tombs 'after His resurrection'—the raising of Jesus triggered the resurrection of these Old Testament believers. The noun denotes the act of raising or awakening, especially from death. Spanish 'resurrección,' French 'résurrection,' and English 'raising' all capture this sense of being brought up from death. This mysterious event demonstrates that Christ's resurrection has corporate implications—His rising inaugurates the general resurrection, beginning with these firstfruits who witness to Jerusalem.

gloss_terse: Spies, secretly planted agents sent to gather information or entrap someone
gloss_readable: This adjective used as a noun means spies or secret agents—people planted to gather information or create a trap. Luke 20:20 describes the religious leaders sending 'spies who pretended to be righteous' to catch Jesus in His words so they could deliver Him to Roman authorities. The term emphasizes their covert, deceptive nature—pretending sincerity while actually seeking to entrap. Classical Greek used it for people secretly inserted into situations for surveillance or subversion. These agents tried to force Jesus into politically dangerous statements.

senses.1: Luke 20:20 records scribes and chief priests sending 'spies' disguised as sincere questioners to trap Jesus with politically dangerous statements about taxes. The term designates secretly planted agents working undercover. English 'spies,' Spanish 'espías,' and French 'espion' all convey this covert surveillance function. Their question about Caesar's tax was designed as a no-win scenario—but Jesus' brilliant 'render to Caesar' response escaped their trap while teaching profound truth about dual citizenship in earthly and heavenly kingdoms.

gloss_terse: Feast of Dedication, Jewish festival commemorating temple rededication by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC
gloss_readable: The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah), an eight-day Jewish festival commemorating the rededication of the temple in 164 BC after Antiochus Epiphanes had desecrated it. Judas Maccabeus cleansed and rededicated the temple following the Maccabean revolt. John 10:22 notes Jesus was in Jerusalem during this feast, walking in Solomon's colonnade during winter. Though not commanded in Torah, this feast celebrated God's faithfulness in restoring temple worship. Jesus' presence there and His claims about being the true temple take on added significance.

senses.1: John 10:22 places Jesus in Jerusalem at the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah), the winter festival celebrating the temple's rededication in 164 BC. The term means 'renewal' or 'consecration.' English 'Dedication,' Spanish 'Dedicación,' French 'dédicace,' and German 'Tempelweihe' all reference this rededication commemoration. Jesus' presence at this feast celebrating restored temple worship sets the stage for His claims to be God's true temple—He is the ultimate fulfillment of what the physical building symbolized.

gloss_terse: Dwelling among, living in the midst of; residing in or with a community
gloss_readable: A participle meaning 'dwelling among' or 'living in the midst of'—residing within or among a group. 2 Peter 2:8 describes righteous Lot 'dwelling among' the people of Sodom, whose lawless deeds tormented his righteous soul. The term emphasizes physical proximity and ongoing residence. Classical Greek used it for inhabiting a place or living among a people. Peter's point is that Lot's geographical location didn't corrupt him—he maintained righteousness despite constant exposure to wickedness, proving God can preserve the godly even in ungodly environments.

senses.1: 2 Peter 2:8 describes righteous Lot 'dwelling among' the Sodomites, whose lawless conduct daily tormented his righteous soul. The participle emphasizes ongoing residence in the midst of a community. Spanish 'habitando' and English 'dwelling' capture this sense of living among a people. Peter uses Lot to demonstrate that God knows how to rescue the godly from trials—Lot maintained righteousness despite prolonged immersion in Sodom's wickedness, showing environmental corruption isn't inevitable for those trusting God.

gloss_terse: To clothe oneself with, put on as a garment; to wrap oneself in or wear something
gloss_readable: This middle voice verb means to clothe oneself with something or put on a garment. 1 Peter 5:5 commands believers to 'clothe yourselves with humility toward one another,' using the imagery of putting on a garment or apron. Classical Greek used it for binding something on oneself or wearing it constantly. Peter's metaphor suggests humility should be as visible and constant as clothing—not an occasional posture but a permanent disposition believers deliberately assume in all relationships. Humility becomes the 'uniform' of Christian community.

senses.1: 1 Peter 5:5 exhorts believers to 'clothe yourselves with humility' toward each other. The middle voice verb means to put on or wrap oneself in something like a garment. Spanish 'vestíos' and English 'clothe yourselves' capture this imagery of deliberately assuming an attitude as one puts on clothing. Peter's command makes humility a visible, constant characteristic—not hidden internal disposition but outward behavior as obvious as the clothes you wear, defining how believers relate to one another in the community.

gloss_terse: Hindrance, obstacle, impediment; something that blocks progress or creates difficulty
gloss_readable: This noun means hindrance, obstacle, or impediment—something that blocks progress or creates difficulty. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 9:12 when explaining why he refuses financial support: 'lest we hinder the gospel of Christ.' The term can refer to physical obstacles or metaphorical barriers. Classical Greek used it for incisions, interruptions, or material obstacles. Paul's concern is pastoral—he'll surrender legitimate rights rather than create any hindrance that might impede the gospel's advance. Nothing must obstruct people from hearing and receiving Christ's message.

senses.1: 1 Corinthians 9:12 explains Paul's refusal of financial support: to avoid putting 'any hindrance in the way of the gospel of Christ.' The noun describes an obstacle or impediment blocking progress. English 'hindrance,' Spanish 'obstáculo,' French 'obstacle,' and German 'Hindernis' all convey this barrier imagery. Paul anticipates critics might accuse him of preaching for money, so he surrenders his apostolic right to support rather than create any stumbling block that might prevent people from receiving the gospel message.

gloss_terse: Self-controlled, disciplined, exercising mastery over desires and impulses; temperate
gloss_readable: This adjective means self-controlled or disciplined—exercising mastery over one's desires, impulses, and appetites. Titus 1:8 lists it among qualifications for elders: they must be self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. Classical Greek used it for those who had power over themselves, masters of their passions. The term emphasizes strength of character that restrains destructive impulses. Leaders must model the self-discipline they call others to practice—controlling tongue, temper, appetites, and ambitions through the Spirit's power.

senses.1: Titus 1:8 requires elders to be 'self-controlled'—exercising disciplined mastery over desires and impulses. The adjective describes someone who has power over themselves, not enslaved to passions. Spanish 'con dominio propio,' French preserves the Greek, and English 'self-disciplined' all emphasize this internal mastery. Church leaders must demonstrate the fruit of the Spirit in personal discipline—their authority over others flows from proven authority over their own appetites, emotions, and impulses through Spirit-empowered character development.
